name: Calvin
tagline: Yale research system for deterministic distributed transactions that commits without two-phase commit.
description: Calvin is a transaction scheduling and replication layer from Daniel Abadi's group at Yale, presented at SIGMOD 2012 by Alexander Thomson, Thaddeus Diamond, Shu-Chun Weng, Kun Ren, Philip Shao and Abadi. Instead of letting partitions and replicas negotiate each commit, a sequencing layer batches incoming transactions into short epochs, agrees on a global order, and replicates that input log; every node then executes transactions deterministically under a lock scheduler that follows the agreed order. Because the outcome is fixed before execution, distributed transactions need no two-phase commit and replicas stay consistent by replaying the same input. The C++ prototype on GitHub mostly backs the VLDB 2014 evaluation of deterministic databases. Calvin's protocol was adopted most visibly by FaunaDB and remains a staple of distributed-transaction research.
statusNote: Academic prototype (2012–2015, Yale, later UMD); code unmaintained. Its protocol influenced FaunaDB and later deterministic databases.

pricing.notes: Source is public on GitHub but carries no open-source license.

scale.notes: Partitions data across nodes and replicates the ordered input log to full replicas, synchronously via Paxos or asynchronously.

strengths: Distributed ACID transactions without two-phase commit by fixing the order before execution
Replication by input log: replicas stay identical by deterministically replaying the same transactions
Showed near-linear throughput scaling for TPC-C-style workloads in the SIGMOD paper
Clear, widely cited design that later systems, notably FaunaDB, built on
weaknesses: Transactions must declare read/write sets up front or run a reconnaissance step first
Epoch batching adds latency to every transaction
Prototype code is unmaintained and not production-ready
notIdealFor: Interactive transactions with unknown read/write sets
